title: Lighthouse eval protocol for cheap configs
content:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight, reproducible evaluation protocol (a.k.a. "Lighthouse") for validating lower-cost serving configurations before they are allowed to be used in production routing. The main goal is to tie objective, low-cost checks to an automated gate so that we can safely expand cheap-config usage without introducing silent quality regressions.

Scope and context:
- Applies to cheap-config variants: lower precision (4-bit/8-bit), trimmed context lengths, smaller model variants (e.g., vicuna-7b -> 4b family), or aggressive KV/prefix cache reductions.
- Intended as a pre-rollout and periodic audit gate for product routes that have an economic target (unit token cost or throughput uplift).
- Complementary to full A/B canaries; this protocol is intentionally small, fast, and inexpensive.

How to use this doc:
- Product owners and engineers should follow the spreadsheet tabs described below and fill in the scenario parameters.
- SRE/Console will run the Lighthouse job (script in linked PR) which uploads results to the rollout dashboard and emits Gate pass/fail.

High-level idea:
1) Define a small stratified eval set that represents critical slices for an endpoint (e.g., short prompts, long-context, multi-turn, JSON-parse). Keep size ~500–2000 examples depending on traffic tier.
2) For each candidate cheap-config, run batched evals and compute a compact set of metrics (quality delta, latency tail change, cost delta).
3) Convert metric deltas into a single economic-risk score (ERS). Compare to preset thresholds that are budget-aware.
4) If ERS < allow_threshold -> gate opens; else fail and require a canary/A/B with manual review.

Spreadsheet model overview (tab descriptions):
- tab: scenario-params -> free-text: route name, traffic % target for cheap-config, baseline model+config, candidate config id, desired unit-cost delta target, date, owner.
- tab: eval-slices -> list of slice names + example counts + sampling weight. Slices must map to production analytics (see linked events).
- tab: raw-results -> per-example baseline/candidate outputs, quality annotations or automatic metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/EMB-sim/LLR), latency, token counts, cost per-example.
- tab: metrics-aggregate -> aggregated metrics per-slice: mean quality, P95 latency, cost per token, percent tokens saved.
- tab: ers-calculation -> the economic-risk score breakdown and final pass/fail decision.
- tab: scenario-sim -> quick scenario simulator to estimate expected # of regressions per 100k tokens given traffic allocation.

Key metrics and formulas (spreadsheet-ready):
- quality-delta(s) = baseline_quality - candidate_quality (higher = worse). Use a mix of automatic metrics plus targeted human anchors.
- latency-p95-delta = candidate_p95 - baseline_p95 (ms).
- cost-delta-percent = (candidate_unit_cost - baseline_unit_cost) / baseline_unit_cost * 100

Economic-risk score (ERS) - conceptual:
ERS = w_q * normalized(quality-delta) + w_l * normalized(latency-p95-delta) + w_c * normalized(cost-delta-percent * -1)
(normalize() maps each metric to a 0-1 scale given scenario priors; cost contributes negatively because we favor cost improvements)

Design choices and recommended default weights (configurable per-route):
- w_q = 0.6 (quality matters most for user satisfaction)
- w_l = 0.2 (latency regressions can cause user-visible harm)
- w_c = 0.2 (we discount cost gains; we require quality first)
- allow_threshold default = 0.25 (ERS below this means candidate is economically acceptable)

Notes on normalization:
- Use historical variance from the slice (30-day rolling) to scale deltas — if quality-deltas are noisy, normalization lowers their influence.
- For small eval sets, cap min-variance to avoid division by tiny numbers.

Sampling plan (practical):
- Base set: 500 examples covering the most frequent slices. For mid-tier routes, 1k. Top-tier product routes: 2k-5k with heavier manual review sample.
- Stratification: sample proportionally to slice traffic but add a minimum 20 examples per slice to detect slice-specific regressions.
- Anchors: include a fixed anchor set (~100 examples) that we run against every candidate to detect subtle drifts across many runs.

Human review budget and where to spend it:
- If automatic metrics show ERS in borderline zone (0.25-0.4) -> surface a 200-example targeted human review focused on highest-impact slices.
- If ERS > 0.4 -> block rollout and require either a rollback of candidate or a targeted model re-tune.

Example scenario (numbers for spreadsheet to copy):
- Baseline: model-x-13b fp16, baseline unit cost $0.015/token, baseline p95 latency 420ms, baseline overall quality score 0.86 (composite).
- Candidate: model-x-13b q4_0 quant, candidate unit cost $0.009/token (40% cheaper), p95 460ms (+40ms), quality score 0.83 (-0.03).
- Normalization (example priors): quality-std = 0.02 -> normalized quality-delta = 1.5 (capped to 1.0);
  latency-std = 25ms -> normalized latency = 1.6 (capped to 1.0);
  cost-delta-percent = -40% -> normalized cost improvement = 0.7.
- ERS = 0.6*1.0 + 0.2*1.0 + 0.2*(1 - 0.7) = 0.6 + 0.2 + 0.06 = 0.86 -> FAIL (too risky despite cost savings).

Operational integration (automation hooks):
- Lighthouse job: a reproducible GitHub Actions / Argo Workflow defined in PR#1723. It checks out the evaluation set, spins up a small runner with a pinned baseline and candidate, runs batched eval, uploads raw-results to the spreadsheet or internal results S3, and emits a gate event.
- Console integration: Gate events turn into rollout decisions — auto-open/auto-block based on ERS and the experimental config in the route.
- Observability: push per-slice metrics to the Console dashboard and to an internal topic for alerting.

Rollback / fallback policies tied to the protocol:
- If a cheap-config is auto-opened but subsequently shows a production regression (weekly eval ERS drift > +0.1) -> automatic throttle of traffic by 50% and notify owners.
- Fast fallback: routes must register a fallback variant (usually baseline or next-mostly-compatible model) that Console can route to within 30s of detection.

Cost vs quality operational heuristics (practical rules):
- Never accept a candidate with quality-delta > 0.05 (absolute) on primary slice unless the route owner signs a waiver.
- Prefer smaller cost deltas with negligible quality impact over large cost wins with borderline quality regression.
- For churn-prone models (nightly fine-tuned checkpoints), tighten allow_threshold by 30%.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Do we include log-prob based calibration checks (LLR) as a mandatory metric or optional slice? Tradeoff: robust but noisy for short prompts.
- How to account for hallucination-specific failure modes? Need a separate hallucination annotation schema and a higher weight for hallucination regressions.
- Where to store long-term historical normalization priors? Suggestion: metrics-priors table in Console DB (ENG-3942 is tracking this).

Action items (owners & rough ETA):
- Jonah: land the Lighthouse runner and CI workflow (PR#1723) — ETA 2026-03-15.
- Priya: produce default slice definitions for top 20 product routes and populate scenario-params template — ETA 2026-03-10 (in review).
- Luca: add gating logic into Console rollout API and visual indicators for ERS — ETA 2026-03-22.
- Maya: finalize spreadsheet template and publish Confluence page with step-by-step guide — ETA 2026-03-12.

Quick checklist for running a Lighthouse job (copyable):
- [ ] pick route and baseline candidate ids in scenario-params tab
- [ ] confirm eval-slices and sample counts
- [ ] run Lighthouse job (GH Action / Argo) with candidate id
- [ ] review metrics-aggregate and ers-calculation tab
- [ ] if borderline, trigger 200-example human review task (assign to QA-group)

Appendix: links to related docs and prior experiments
- Prior economic calibration experiments: /product/optimize/anchor-eval-cost-model-experiments.json
- Regression budgeting notes: /product/optimize/regression-risk-budgeting-scenarios.json
- Related PRs: https://github.com/redwood-inference/ops/pull/1723

Notes to reviewers (informal):
- This is deliberately conservative on quality; we had a few customer incidents where a 0.02 quality drop on a named slice materially harmed downstream conversions. The spreadsheet is intentionally opinionated but configurable per-route.
- Feedback requested on normalization choices and the default thresholds — particularly from SRE (latency tolerance) and Solutions Eng (slice definitions).
